lesson.title: Motion Takes être
lesson.subtitle: je suis allé(e), elle est venue, il est parti — the motion verbs that take être in the past and agree like adjectives

hook.title: Why 'I Went' Is Literally 'I Am Gone'
hook.content: Think of old English sentences like 'He is risen', 'The summer is gone', or 'Babylon is fallen'. Why did English use 'is' instead of 'has' there? Because those verbs don't act on an outside object — they change the state or location of the speaker! French kept that exact rule for a cozy house of whole-body motion and doorway verbs: aller (allé 'gone'), venir (venu 'come'), arriver (arrivé 'arrived'), partir (parti 'left'), sortir (sorti 'gone out'), monter (monté 'gone up'), descendre (descendu 'gone down'), rester (resté 'stayed'), tomber (tombé 'fallen'), and naître (né 'born').

footnotes.title: Picture a house with a front door and stairs
footnotes.content: Instead of memorizing an acronym like DR & MRS VANDERTRAMP, picture one house: you approach it (aller/venir), cross the threshold (arriver/partir, entrer/sortir), take the stairs (monter/descendre, tomber), stay inside (rester), and live your life cycle (naître/mourir)!

pattern.title: Inside the être House, the Participle Wears Gender and Number
pattern.content: Because je suis allé literally means 'I am gone', the participle behaves just like an adjective after être! If the speaker is a woman, she writes an extra silent -e: Je suis allée, elle est venue, elle est partie. If the subject is plural, add a silent -s: Nous sommes arrivés (or -es for a group of women: Elles sont arrivées). In sound, allé, allée, allés, allées are 100% identical (/ale/) — only your pen adds the badge!
pattern.linguist_note: Intransitive unaccusative verbs in Latin (nātus sum, reversus sum) formed their perfect with esse and agreed with the subject; French and Italian preserved this split auxiliary system.
pattern.trap_note: The shortcut your mind will offer: saying *J'ai allé for 'I went'. Motion-and-doorway verbs ALWAYS take être: Je suis allé(e)!

exercises.prompt: Match each être-house past participle with its opposite partner:
exercises.target_answer: venu (come), parti (left / departed), descendu (gone down), resté (stayed), tombé (fallen)
exercises.meaning: allé (gone), arrivé (arrived), monté (gone up), sorti (gone out), né (born)
exercises.explanation: Notice how the être house is organized in natural spatial pairs!

exercises.prompt: What is the literal word-for-word structure of 'Elle est arrivée hier'?
exercises.meaning: Literal structure: She is arrived yesterday
exercises.explanation: Because arriver is an être-house motion verb, French says 'She is arrived' with feminine -e on arrivée.

exercises.prompt: Marie is speaking: how does she write 'I went to the café'?
exercises.meaning: I went to the café (female speaker)
exercises.explanation: aller takes être (je suis), and a female speaker adds feminine -e: allée.

cues: She came (is come, feminine) → Elle est venue + with her brother → avec son frère
exercises.target_answer: Elle est venue avec son frère
exercises.explanation: venir takes être, and elle adds feminine -e to venu → venue.

diagnosis.slip: used a instead of est or forgot -e on venue
diagnosis.cue: venir takes être and agrees with Elle: Elle est venue.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
cues: He is left: Il est parti
exercises.explanation: partir takes être: Il est parti.
exercises.affirmation: You used est parti and ce matin cleanly.

summary.outcome: Form the passé composé of motion and doorway verbs using être and agree the participle with the subject in writing.

use_example.german: Je suis allé à la gare et elle est venue avec moi.
use_example.english: I went to the station and she came with me.

summary.takeaway: Whole-body motion and doorway verbs take être ('I am gone'), and their participle agrees with the traveller.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on Le Pont ([1801] The être House): see how Motion Takes être leads directly into The être House.

twist.prompt: Ungraded — 'We stayed here' (masculine plural: Nous sommes restés):
twist.explanation: rester ('to stay') lives in the être house, and plural nous adds -s to restés.

foreshadow.line: Having mastered Motion Takes être, look ahead to Topic 19 (The Storytelling Past), where this machinery expands into the next dimension of French thought.

payoff.text: The foundation from Topic 17 (The -é Past) now pays off directly inside Motion Takes être: every sentence here builds on that earlier step.

allé.etymology_derivation: aller's participle; motion verbs form their past with être — and the participle agrees: allée, allés, allées.

arrivé.etymology_derivation: Late Latin ad rīpam 'to the shore' — to arrive was to land on a riverbank.

venu.etymology_derivation: Latin venīre — venue (where you come), venture, adventure (what you come to).

parti.etymology_derivation: partir takes être in the past: je suis parti(e).

sorti.context_phrase: Elle est sortie avec ses amis.
sorti.context_translation: She went out with her friends.
sorti.etymology_derivation: sortir takes être in the past.

monté.etymology_derivation: Latin montem 'mountain' — to go up is to mountain-ward.

resté.etymology_derivation: Latin restāre 'to stand back, remain'. Staying counts as motion's family — être-house logic.

né.etymology_derivation: Latin nātus — natal, native, nation (the born-together people).

être.etymology_derivation: Latin esse 'to be' → essere → être. English kept the root in essence and quintessential — the being-ness inside the word.

suis.etymology_derivation: je suis is literally 'I follow' — Latin sequor, the root of sequence and sequel. Being is following, historically.

ion.name: The -ION Bridge
ion.phonetic_rule: Spelling converts 1:1; the final N is nasalised — thought, not said (collection /kɔlɛksjɔ̃/).
ion.historical_linguistics: English absorbed thousands of Latin-dress nouns through Norman French and later Renaissance borrowing. The -tion/-sion endings are the single largest cognate landing zone between the two languages.
ion.philological_note: Every -ION noun is feminine, so the article is la — elided to l' before a vowel. The ending is a gender decoder, not a memory item.
ion.literature_source: Walter, Le français dans tous les sens (1988); Pope, From Latin to Modern French (1952).

ation.name: The -ation Engine
ation.historical_linguistics: French -er verbs descend from Latin -āre; the English -ation nouns and French verbs are two leaves of the same Latin branch, so the noun unlocks the verb with almost no loss.
ation.philological_note: The whole -ation goes — célébration → célébrer, never *célébrater. Test for the -ation noun in English first; it is the proof the verb converts.
ation.literature_source: Guillaume, Temps et verbe (1929); standard French morphophonology.

ite.name: The -ité Bridge
ite.phonetic_rule: English final -ity becomes stressed final -ité /ite/ — the é marks the syllable English swallows.
ite.historical_linguistics: Latin -itās survives in English -ity and French -ité; both are bookish layers grafted onto the everyday vocabulary, which is why they convert with no sound loss.
ite.philological_note: All -ité nouns are feminine (la possibilité, la liberté).
ite.literature_source: Pope (1952); Brunot, Histoire de la langue française.

ance.name: The -ance/-ence Twins
ance.phonetic_rule: Same spelling family; the AN is nasal: différence /difeʁɑ̃s/.
ance.historical_linguistics: Latin -antia/-entia produced English -ance/-ence and French -ance/-ence directly; the pair is one of the highest-conversion zones in the vocabulary.

e.name: The é/ed Twins
e.phonetic_rule: The past participle in -é /e/ is the English -ed: mangé/manged, décidé/decided, marié/married.
e.historical_linguistics: The Norman conquest put French participles straight into English verb morphology — countless English past tenses ARE French participles wearing English spelling.
e.philological_note: With avoir, the participle never agrees; with être (motion verbs), it does — the one agreement the past asks for.
e.literature_source: Baugh & Cable, A History of the English Language (2002).

ment.name: The -ment Adverb Bridge
ment.phonetic_rule: English -ly adverbs convert to -ment: exactement, rapidement — the ME is nasal, like pain.
ment.historical_linguistics: Latin -mente ('in a ... mind') became French -ment and English kept the same suffix for nouns (moment, comment) — but French built adverbs with it where English built them with -ly.
ment.philological_note: Feminine adjectives get an -e before -ment: exacte → exactement.

eur.name: The -eur Bridge
eur.phonetic_rule: Latin -or/-er nouns convert to -eur /œʁ/: doctor → docteur, color → couleur.
eur.historical_linguistics: The agent and quality suffixes of Latin split three ways in English (-or, -er, -our) but re-merge in French as -eur.
eur.philological_note: -eur is usually masculine — couleur and erreur are the famous rebels. The lesson names the exceptions before you trust the rule blindly.

able.name: The -able Bridge
able.phonetic_rule: Adjectives in -able/-ible convert as-is: adorable, possible, invisible — only the stress moves.
able.historical_linguistics: Latin -ābilis/-ibilis landed in both languages with the spelling intact; it is the highest-fidelity conversion family in the whole bridge.
able.philological_note: Same form, different stress: invisible with the beat on the final syllable in French.

doublet.name: Norman Doublets
doublet.phonetic_rule: Same Latin word entered English twice — once Germanic-dressed, once Norman: warden/gardien, estate/état, hôtel/hospital.
doublet.historical_linguistics: After 1066 English borrowed Norman French wholesale; centuries of independent drift mean many English words have a French twin that looks different and sounds different but is the same word.
doublet.philological_note: French dropped Latin H everywhere (hôtel, homme) and dropped S before consonants (état, école) — the dropped letters are the fingerprints.
